items.title: feat(benchmarks): patch-quality benchmark for LLM-generated code
items.body:
Adds `benchmarks/patch-quality/`, a benchmark that scores SWE-bench Verified patches for **maintainability** rather than correctness, comparing each model submission against the commit a human maintainer actually wrote for the same issue.

It backs the claim in the repo's own tagline. polyscan is "code quality analyzers for AI agents"; this measures the code quality of AI agents.

No model APIs are called. Every patch already exists as a published leaderboard submission, so a full run costs nothing but disk and time.

## What it measures

```
git checkout base_commit
analyze the files the patch touches      -> before
git apply the patch
analyze the same files                   -> after
delta = after - before
```

Only complexity and dead code. Both are computed per function from the CFG of a single file, so they stay exact when only part of a repository is analyzed. Coupling, cohesion, clone and dependency metrics need the whole codebase and would undercount on a subset, making each score depend on which files a patch happened to touch.

"Worse" is judged **per function**, comparing each function against itself. The maximum complexity over a set of files is nearly useless here: django's `sql/query.py` holds a 21-branch method, so nothing a patch does to a 4-branch method next to it moves the file's maximum at all.

## Result over django (231 instances, 14 submissions + human)

3 of 14 models regress more often than the human patch at p<0.05, and **2 survive Bonferroni correction** across 14 comparisons: `gpt-5` (p=0.001) and `devstral-small` (p=0.000), both OpenHands. They sit at opposite ends of that group's resolve rate, so this is not a capability ordering.

The other 12, including the entire controlled scaffold group, are indistinguishable from the human baseline. A typical model raises some measured metric on 29–58 of its 110–168 gated instances against 19–43 for the human on those same instances — the two sides move together, because most of what drives a regression is the issue rather than who fixed it. That is the argument for pairing, and for extending past django to the other eleven repositories.

`report.py` pairs each model against the human on shared instances and runs an exact McNemar test, because ratios built on this many events mislead.

## Four traps, and why the code is not fifty lines

Each of these silently turns a broken patch into an apparent quality improvement.

**The analyzer's own defaults decide what gets measured.** `pyscn --min-complexity` defaults to 5, and it filters the *reported function list*, not just a display threshold. Left at the default, django's `sql/query.py` reports 29 functions summing to 277 complexity when the file actually holds 105 summing to 425 — 72% of functions invisible. Worse, the threshold breaks monotonicity in both directions: a function simplified from 6 to 4 drops out of the report and reads as a *deleted function*, which also feeds the destructive heuristic, while one that grows from 3 to 8 appears from nowhere with no "before" value to compare against. The harness pins `--min-complexity 1`.

The general problem outlives that flag: absence of metrics for a file is ambiguous between "has no functions" and "the analyzer declined to look". pyscn excludes `test_*.py`, and 65 django records were padding their file and line counts with code nobody measured. The analyzer adapter cross-checks its own parse against the report and returns the difference as `skipped_files`.

**Created and deleted files are asymmetric.** Agents leave scratch files behind (`check_url_parts.py`, `final_verification.py`). They have no "before" state but do get measured "after", so every delta inflates. Deletion is the same problem pointing the other way and easier to miss: a removed file *has* a "before" measurement and no "after", so leaving it in the measured set books its entire complexity as an improvement. Renames are a delete plus a create. The harness measures only paths present on both sides and counts the rest separately. The created-file count tracks the agent scaffold rather than the model, ranging from 0 to over 5 scratch files per solved issue.

**A file that does not parse scores perfectly.** No parse means no functions, which means no complexity and no dead code. One submission corrupted `django/db/models/sql/query.py` with `return 0 objs`; it went from 105 functions and 425 total complexity to zero and zero, and ranked as the single largest quality improvement in the run until this was caught. Across django, 71 of 3407 records are patches that broke a file they touched; `o4-mini` and `qwen2.5-coder-32b` account for 47.

The harness gets there two ways on purpose. pyscn reports unparseable files in `complexity.Errors`, but matching that is matching on message text, which is not an interface — if the wording ever changes the defence fails silently and in the worst direction. So every measured file is also parsed with `ast`. Neither source is trusted alone, and both are applied differentially: a file that already failed to parse *before* the patch is not blamed on the patch.

**Mass deletion passes the syntax check.** The same submission deleted 2,124 of 2,671 lines from that file elsewhere, and the result was still valid Python. Parsing cannot catch it. Every such case in the django run was `unresolved`, so the correctness gate is the only defence. The harness flags them `destructive` and the report excludes flagged pairs rather than averaging them in — a gutted file is not evidence of clean code, and counting it as a *non*-regression would drag the model's rate down.

## The correctness gate changes the answer

`--resolved-only` restricts each model to the instances it actually solved. Over django, 8 of 14 models look worse than the human patch at p<0.05 without the gate; 3 do with it.

Most of that gap is survivorship. A patch that fails its tests is often failing because it broke or gutted something, and broken code has less measurable complexity than working code, so ungated numbers credit failure as simplification. The outcome columns catch the blatant cases — `broke_syntax`, `not_a_diff`, `destructive` — but nothing short of running the tests catches a patch that is syntactically fine and semantically wrong.

What the gate does *not* buy is a clean read on capability. Among the seven models in the controlled scaffold group, resolve rate and regression rate correlate at r = +0.87 once gated. That is not "stronger models write messier code": a model that solves more instances is being measured on harder ones, and harder issues take larger patches. Instance difficulty is not controlled for, which is exactly why the report pairs against the human on *the same* instances instead of comparing rates across models.

## Comparing models fairly

Submissions differ by scaffold, retry policy and prompt, not only by model. `config/models.json` tags each with a `scaffold` and the report groups by it; the `mini-swe-agent-v1.0.0` group is seven models through an identical harness, so the model is the only variable.

Directory names also lie: `20250516_cortexa_o3` is not o3, it is NVIDIA's Nemotron-CORTEXA, an ensemble over a dozen models with 2+ attempts. That is noted in the config.

## Notes for review

- **Zero dependencies**, stdlib only. PyYAML was not available so config is JSON. 41 stdlib unit tests cover the diff parsing, the statistics and the report extraction; CI runs them plus ruff.
- `data/` (~99 MB) and `repos/` are gitignored and reproducible from the two fetch scripts. The django result set is committed gzipped, 1.5 MB of JSONL down to ~110 KB, so `python3 report.py results/django.jsonl.gz --resolved-only` reproduces the numbers without running anything — and works from a clean checkout, because the correctness gate travels inside the result set rather than being read back out of the gitignored `data/`. Each result set opens with a metadata record naming the analyzer build that produced it.
- 117 of `qwen2.5-coder-32b`'s "patches" are the stderr of a failed git command rather than diffs. They get their own `not_a_diff` outcome instead of looking like a patch that touched no Python.
- Model patches are **not** in the `swe-bench/experiments` GitHub repo despite its README documenting `all_preds.jsonl`. At HEAD there are zero and only four ever existed in history. `fetch_data.py` pulls them from the `swe-bench-submissions` S3 bucket, which is publicly readable with a prefix.
- `analyzer.py` exposes one interface. Adding jscan against SWE-bench Multilingual means implementing `run()`; nothing in the harness is Python-specific.

## Related

Building this surfaced two pyscn issues:

- [ludo-technologies/pyscn#690](https://github.com/ludo-technologies/pyscn/issues/690) — `pyscn check` exits 0 and reports Grade A on code with syntax errors, which is trap 3 seen from the analyzer side
- [ludo-technologies/pyscn#689](https://github.com/ludo-technologies/pyscn/issues/689) — exponential blowup in dependency analysis. Not hit here because the benchmark only selects complexity and deadcode, but it is why whole-repository measurement was rejected as an approach.

A third is worth filing: `--min-complexity` silently filtering the reported function list makes any before/after diff non-monotonic, and the flag reads as a display threshold.

## Summary
Two related changes: (1) fix a fan-out in the `behavior_scores` extraction that inflated `numerator`/`denominator` ~100–300×, and (2) enable the 12 new sentiment behaviors end-to-end.

### 1. Fan-out fix
`behavior_scores.sql` built its spine from `expert_performance_metrics` (epm) and `LEFT JOIN`ed the observe scores on `(expert_id, date)`. **epm is a tall per-metric table** (one row per expert/date/metric), so the row-level join multiplied every behavior by that expert's metric-count for the day.

- `calc`/rates are **unchanged** (the fan-out preserved ratios); only absolute volumes are corrected. Scoring was correct-by-accident before (engine scores on `calc`, and confidence's denom floor saturated regardless).

items.title: feat(logic_vista): add LogicVista visual logical reasoning benchmark
items.body:
## What

Integrates [`evalscope/LogicVista`](https://modelscope.cn/datasets/evalscope/LogicVista/summary) ([paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.04973)) — 448 visual multiple-choice items testing inductive / deductive / numerical / spatial / mechanical reasoning — as a native VLM benchmark.

## Design

LogicVista draws its answer options **inside the image**, so there is no textual choice list to render. The adapter reuses `MultiChoiceAdapter` for the answer parsing path but builds its own message content, exactly as `visulogic` does; `choices` only carries the label alphabet that `parse_answers` validates against. No new registry, loader or scoring machinery — `acc` and the base `match_score` cover it.

Two details were derived from the data and from the reference implementations (official `eval/extract_accuracy.py`, VLMEvalKit `dataset/utils/logicvista.py`) rather than assumed:

- **Label range is not A–D.** It varies per question and reaches A–I (`"Select answers from A-I"`), so the alphabet is 9 letters. With the usual 4-letter alphabet, item `v1_4` (target `G`) would have been silently discarded by the parser and scored 0 — a real run confirms it now scores correctly.
- **Three items are multi-select** (ground truth like `A, C`), which both reference implementations compare as an unordered set. `multiple_correct` is enabled and targets are normalized to the same sorted, separator-free form `extract_answer` emits (`A, C` → `AC`).

Two released items cannot be scored as published, and both are stated in the description so they aren't mistaken for harness bugs:

- `v1_382` has neither a question nor an answer → skipped (447 evaluated).
- `v1_20` labels its options with digits (`1-5`), which no letter-based parser can match. The official GPT-4 extractor and VLMEvalKit's judge (`res.isalpha()`) reject it the same way.

## Verification

`qwen-vl-plus`, 100 items (20 per skill), `max_tokens=2048`:

```
acc=0.5700  answer-line-present=99/100
{'deductive': '12/20', 'inductive': '6/20', 'mechanical': '18/20', 'numerical': '18/20', 'spatial': '3/20'}
```

Every stored score was re-derived from the raw completion with an independent parser. The single divergence is one reply truncated before its answer line, where the framework falls back to the last capital letter and happened to guess right — hence the description asks for a generous `max_tokens`. Per-skill counts sum to the sample total, and the shape (numerical/mechanical high, spatial/inductive low) matches the paper's reported spread.

## Tests

- `tests/benchmark/test_vlm.py`: `test_logic_vista` (real API) and `test_logic_vista_mock`.
- `tests/benchmark/test_logic_vista.py`: unit tests pinning target normalization, multi-select round-tripping, out-of-alphabet rejection, skipping of items without ground truth, and the guarantee that a model echoing the prompt cannot have that echo scored as a valid label.

Also run: `make lint`, `pytest tests/cli/test_all.py::TestRun::test_ci_lite`, `make docs-pipeline BENCHMARK=logic_vista FORCE=1` (docs and `_meta` are generated, regenerated after the final prompt wording).

## Summary

Progresses #197.

This is the Adaptive ASK selection-control slice only. It adds a deterministic pre-result selection seal for one existing Adaptive materialized case; it does not invoke Codex or Claude, collect outputs, resume execution, score results, aggregate telemetry, or run a measured benchmark.

## Selection and seal contract

- `seal-selection` accepts an existing plan, materialized root, external state directory, Adaptive case ID, and normalized selection input. It never generates a plan or rematerializes a case.
- `verify-selection` independently revalidates the same binding and writes nothing.
- The sealed record binds `plan_id`, canonical plan digest, materialization-manifest digest, output-root identity, materializer version/revision, case/block/adapter/condition/fixture/repetition identity, frozen-input digest, condition-projection digest, projection fingerprint, and normalized selection payload.
- It is Adaptive-only: Plain, Kernel-only, Full ASK, missing, stale, cross-plan, cross-case, and cross-adapter attempts fail closed.
- A shared result-artifact detector rejects `.benchmark-*`, normalized output/result, score, and telemetry artifacts before sealing and during verification.

## State and digest boundary

- State lives only outside agent-visible cases at `<state-dir>/selections/<case-id>.json`.
- `<state-dir>/selection-state.json` is a versioned identity/index tied to one plan and materialization; it records prior seals, so deletion cannot enable recreation.
- State roots reject regular files, undeclared entries, case-root placement, and symlink traversal. Publication uses staging plus no-replace selection creation and atomic index replacement; incomplete staging is removed. Read-only mode is tamper evidence, not administrator-proof security.
- `selection_digest` is SHA-256 of recursively key-sorted canonical JSON with `selection_digest` omitted. Array order remains semantic, unique arrays reject duplicates, caller-provided digests are rejected, and every binding-field change changes the digest.

## Materialization consumer validation

Before sealing or verifying, the consumer revalidates the supplied plan and manifest Schema plus plan/config/protocol/repository/materializer identities; exact plan-case namespace; case count; unique case and condition identities; four-condition blocks; adapter/profile/projection relationships; actual case inventories, bytes, modes, and digests; projection boundaries; evaluator exclusion; and path/symlink gates. Manifest status strings are not trusted by themselves.

## Selection semantics

- Lightweight bypass requires a non-empty reason, no selected mechanisms, and explicit skipped mechanisms. An empty ordinary selection is rejected.
- Capability downgrades retain capability and reason, cannot also be selected mechanisms, do not substitute adapters, and do not score unavailable runtime capability as zero.
- The sealed schema rejects result, correctness, score, recommendation, completion, hidden-test, oracle, evaluator, and unknown fields.

Legacy B/B2/C and materialization coverage remains in the existing tests without fixture/result contract changes.

items.title: RMB-A: add Riya model benchmark foundation
items.body:
# RMB-A: add Riya model benchmark foundation

Provider-neutral, offline, **evidence-only** contracts for future model benchmarking. Baseline `359fc4b09a84573a0862c52fd7ac582b4e9fa995`.

**No model has been benchmarked, selected, downloaded, invoked or recommended.** Every identifier in the fixtures is invented (`model.alpha`, `release.beta`, `engine.gamma`), and no number here describes anything real.

---

## Three evidence authorities, deliberately not merged

| Authority | Package | Owns |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Safety | `@qf-jarvis/model-evaluation` | generic safety and red-team |
| Quality | `@qf-jarvis/riya-quality-evaluation` | Riya sales quality (P10) |
| Operational | `@qf-jarvis/riya-model-benchmark` | latency, decode speed, request success, memory |

The obvious next step from three sets of numbers is one weighted score, and it is the mistake this design exists to prevent: latency, quality and safety have no shared unit, so a weighting is a business judgement that stops looking like one once it is arithmetic. A fast model with a bad refusal rate would outrank a slower correct one, defensibly, because the spreadsheet said so.

**No composite score, no winner, no rank, no recommendation, no approval â€” and no Pareto relation.** A dominance verdict needs every axis present on both sides, and memory is optional; an unmeasured axis silently drops out, so `EQUIVALENT` could mean "equal on the axes we happened to share" â€” a finding about what the harness recorded, phrased as a finding about two configurations. Comparison returns named parity mismatches and side-by-side deltas. **An axis absent from the deltas was not compared**, and nothing summarises that away.

## Verification, not hash comparison

`sha256OfCanonical` is unkeyed. Anyone who can edit an artifact can recompute the digest over the edit, so a self-consistent hash proves only that the body and the digest were written by the same hand â€” **hash self-consistency is not schema validity**.

`verifyRiyaBenchmarkEvidence` and `verifyRiyaBenchmarkResultSet` therefore **reconstruct**: full canonical surface required, unknown keys refused at every level, each nested object rebuilt through its own constructor, cross-field invariants re-proved, digests recomputed from the reconstruction. An attacker who recomputes the digest over a structurally impossible artifact still fails.

A **stored** artifact must carry its whole surface â€” including `syntheticWorkload: true`, `productionApproval: false` and the digest. The constructor lets a caller omit those when building something new; the verifier may not fill in a blank, or a stored artifact missing `productionApproval` would come back with `false` supplied by the verifier rather than by whoever wrote the file. Neither verifier restamps.

Both boolean helpers are total: `unknown` in, boolean out, never a throw.

## Comparison verifies its inputs first

Both sets are verified before anything is read, and only the reconstructions are used. A comparison that reads an untrusted object produces output indistinguishable from a real answer â€” and that output is what somebody pastes into a decision. An invalid input yields no comparison object at all.

## A result set is one configuration, many workload cases

| Uniform across the set | Free to vary per case |
| --- | --- |
| entire subject | `workloadCaseId` |
| entire environment | prompt profile digest, input tokens, output cap |
| suite id / version | concurrency, batch size |
| harness id / version | warmup and measured counts |
| `measurementPolicyRef` | streaming, sampling config |

Homogeneity on subject and environment is what makes a set a claim about something real; without it one case could be measured on one model and another on a different one, and the aggregate would describe a machine that does not exist. Equality is by SHA-256 over the canonical form, not a field list that stops covering a field the moment somebody adds one.

Case **shape** is meant to vary â€” `short/c1`, `long/c1`, `short/c8`, `short/c32` are four cases of one suite, and throughput under **rising** concurrency is unmeasurable by a set permitted to hold one concurrency. What must not vary is who measured and by what rules.

**Two levels:** intra-set, diverse cases under one harness; inter-set, pair by `workloadCaseId` then require exact workload parity for that pair.

## Exact identity everywhere

No `latest` at any `/` segment, case-insensitively — across **every durable ref in the artifact**: the release; `promptFamily`, `capabilityProfileRef`, `knowledgeRevision`, `policyContractRevision`; `benchmarkSuiteId`, `benchmarkImplementationId`, `workloadCaseId`, `measurementPolicyRef`; and, when supplied, `acceleratorRef`, `runtimeEngineId`, `runtimeEngineVersion`.

`promptFamily: 'latest'` names a prompt that changes under the evidence, and `measurementPolicyRef: 'latest'` names rules that have since changed — the release failure, one field along. Benchmark evidence is quoted months later against runs nobody remembers, so a moving alias anywhere in it is invisible in the number it accompanies.

Not applied to versions, digests, enums or `createdAt`: a numeric version cannot be an alias, and a SHA-256 already names exact content.

The predicate is exported from `model-evaluation` as `isExactGovernedIdentity` and imported rather than restated — through a single internal re-export, so this package's import boundary stays one line wide — and "exact" therefore has one definition. Governance, not grammar: `PROVIDER_MODEL_ID_PATTERN` is untouched, and a ref merely *containing* the substring (`policy-latest-v2`) stays legal. The same pass closed two omissions in `createEvaluationBinding` â€” `knowledgeRevision` and `redTeamSuiteId` were absent from its wildcard loop.

## Observation checks that matter

A broken harness produces plausible numbers, not obviously wrong ones.

- Requests must balance; percentiles must be ordered.
- **A run with zero successes cannot claim latency.** Total failure produces the most flattering numbers a harness can emit â€” instant time-to-first-token, because there were no tokens. A total-failure run is still representable; it just has no latency.
- Tokens and decode speed must agree about whether output happened.
- Canonical instants are validated arithmetically, leap-aware. `Date.parse('2026-02-30T00:00:00Z')` returns a finite number and normalizes to March.

## Environment

items.title: docsy: search-quality benchmark (query set, answer key, eval)
items.body:
Measures docs search against real user queries, so a search change can be **shown** to help and quality cannot decay unnoticed. Implements **DOC-1397** under **DOC-1254**.

Split out of the combined indexer PR: this runs **on demand with a human in the loop**, not per deploy, and should not gate the security fix (DOC-1285) which needs only the indexer.

## Not build CI — and deliberately so

| lifecycle | what | automated? |
|---|---|---|
| every deploy | the indexer (separate PR) | yes |
| every content PR | `make check-search-labels` — path existence, no network | **yes** (companion: unionai-docs#1399) |
| on demand / periodic | the eval itself | **no** — needs LLM judgment and human correction |

## Contents

| tool | does |
|---|---|
| `find_candidates` | expanded-term search over content |
| `digest_candidates` | compact page digests, so canonicality is judged from prose not scores |
| `draft_ideals` | first-pass labels |
| `eval_search` | MRR@10 / Recall@5 / nDCG@10 / **Pages@10** / zero-rate |
| `check_labels` | validates a key; wired to `make check-search-labels` |
| `diff_labels` | classifies key changes as content- vs judgment-driven |
| `queries.judged.json` | **45 real queries**, per-facet, multi-ideal, human-corrected |

## Three findings baked into the design

**Candidate ranking needs two signals.** Breadth alone found `gpu` (the canonical "Resources" page hits 9/9 expansion terms; a tutorial saying "gpu" *more often* hits 1/9) but broke `secret` (a CI/CD guide mentions secret, credential, api key **and** password). Canonicality alone is biased *against* canonical pages, which are titled with the general concept while users type the specific term.

**Labels are per-facet and multi-valued.** Search returns four groups, so a flat label scores a grouped result list wrong — and one label per group makes *correct* results register as misses.

**Absolute scores are not a quality claim.** The key carries judgment error: of five labels a human reviewed, four changed. Valid for comparing arms against a shared key; not for grading search in absolute terms. The eval says so in its output.

## What it has already found

- **Result dilution** — `task environment` returned 8 hits that were all one page. Fixed in the indexer PR; measured **Pages@10 4.52 → 9.68** over 50 real queries.
- **`/docs/latest/*` search returns nothing** — likely inflating the no-result rate in DOC-1237.
- **Vocabulary gaps** — `deck`, `shelltask`, `eager`, `flytectl`, `map_task` all have good v2 pages behind a renamed term.
- **Genuine content gaps** — `maxmessagesizebytes`, `eventspublisher` have no page at all.

## Known gap

`eval_search.py` still reads `ideal` as a flat list, from before the per-group schema. Needs updating before the arms produce real MRR/nDCG; the label-free metrics (Pages@10, zero-rate) work today.

items.body:
Fourteen commits that accumulated on this branch. They fall into four independent groups; the benchmark work is the largest and is entirely inert until a flag is set.

## 1. API-Football Prediction Benchmark (new feature, ships disabled)

An external, read-only benchmark of our own recommendation against API-Football's `/predictions` endpoint. **It cannot affect predictions**: the module never imports `PredictionEngine`, `confidence`, `value`, or any pipeline stage, and it runs out-of-band on a cron, reading `predictions_history` rows written minutes-to-hours earlier.

- `server-utils/predictionBenchmark/` — provider, normalizer, deterministic consensus comparator, persistence, sweep orchestrator
- `supabase/migrations/039_prediction_benchmarks.sql` — new table, service-role-only RLS (`using(false)`)
- `api/backtest.js` — four gated read views (`benchmark-summary`, `-by-market`, `-head-to-head`, `-agreement-rate`)
- `api/cron/daily-ml.js?mode=prediction-benchmark-sweep` — folded into an existing route to stay under the Vercel Hobby 12-function cap
- `src/components/admin/BenchmarkPanel.tsx` — admin-only dashboard
- `docs/PREDICTION_BENCHMARK_RESEARCH.md` — field-by-field research

Gated behind `PREDICTION_BENCHMARK_ENABLED`, which is **unset in production**. Until it is set, the cron returns `{ok: true, skipped: "flag_disabled"}`.

### Defects found and fixed by running it against live data

The original implementation shipped against the *documented* contract without a live response ever being captured. A probe against fixture 1607560 then two 30-fixture sweeps exposed four real defects, all fixed here:

| | Defect | Impact |
|---|---|---|
| A | Uncovered fixtures return a null winner and a placeholder `33/33/33` percent triple. The tie-insensitive reducer kept the first entry, fabricating a Home pick at 33% | **27 of 30 swept fixtures** would have been phantom home picks counted as real disagreements |
| B | `last_5.att`/`.def` arrive as percent strings (`"38%"`); `Number()` gave `NaN` and nulled them | Silent data loss on every row |
| C | `tipMarketFamily` collapses all O/U lines into one `ou` bucket, so a corners pick (`Over 7.5`) could line up against API-Football's goals number. The authoritative `recommended.family` was already being passed in and thrown away | 15 of 30 rows misclassified |
| E | The already-benchmarked skip queried `schema_version = "benchmark-v1"` but persists `"afb-v1"`, so it never matched | ~3x redundant upstream calls per run |
| F | `Number(null)` is `0`, not `NaN`, so a null `winner.id` stored as `teamId: 0` | Latent: reads as "API named a team" to any `!= null` check |

### Known limitations, deliberately not addressed

- **API-Football covers ~2 of our ~10 market families.** Only `winner` and `percent` are structurally reliable; BTTS/DC come from a best-effort regex over free-text `advice`; corners, cards, shots, correct score and first-half have no counterpart at all.
- **No pricing.** The payload carries no odds or EV, so provider-side ROI is deliberately not computed — `benchmarkEvents.js` documents why rather than fabricating a price.
- **Currently 0 comparable rows.** The 3-day sweep window presently covers only week-one European qualifiers, where API-Football has no model output for 27/30 fixtures. Expected to improve once domestic leagues start; the feature is not worth surfacing in user-facing UI until measured.
- The MatchModal consensus row and `ConsensusBlock.tsx` are built but **not wired** — `MatchModal.tsx` passes `null` by construction.

## 2. Special Bet hardening

One-per-family selection tightened, and goals lines now restricted to those that actually have book odds, so legs can no longer be correlated or unpriced.

## 3. MatchModal information architecture

Restructured into a single Decision Layer, removing a duplicated pick/odds/confidence block from the score header. Adds `MarketFamilyIcon` and `formatRecommendation.ts`.

## 4. Odds and live-momentum fixes

Shots-on-target and total-shots book odds now resolve and display; live momentum stays stable across empty stats polls.

## Repo hygiene

`graphify-out/` (86 files) and `.impeccable/` were tracked, contributing 77,291 of the original 80,999 insertions and making this diff unreviewable. Both are local agent tooling artifacts and now join the existing ignore section beside `.codegraph/`, `.codex/`, `.serena/` and `.cursor/`. Files remain on disk; only tracking is removed.

- [x] `npm run typecheck` — clean
- [x] `npm run lint` — no new findings on touched paths
- [x] Migrations 038 + 039 applied; `prediction_benchmarks` verified present
- [x] Two live sweeps: 30 scanned / 30 persisted / 0 errors; dedupe verified skipping already-swept fixtures
- [x] Defect fixes verified against stored rows (`our_family` reclassified 20 `ou` → 15 `corners` + 5 `ou`; zero rows carrying `teamId: 0`)
- [ ] **Reviewer:** confirm the UI changes in groups 2–4 — those are user-facing and were verified visually, not by automated test
- [ ] **Reviewer:** decide whether `PREDICTION_BENCHMARK_ENABLED` should be set in production on merge, or left off until leagues are underway

## Rollback

The benchmark is inert without its env var, so group 1 needs no rollback. Groups 2–4 are independent commits and can be reverted individually.

items.body:
## Context

This came up during benchmark testing. The generated and scored task counts matched the dataset size, but some submission files still contained null attempt slots from provider timeouts. Those nulls count as incorrect during scoring even though the model never produced a usable response.

The configured attempt count is intended to give the model a fair number of chances on every test pair. Before this change, resume mode considered a task complete as soon as its submission file existed. A task with one valid response and one timeout therefore remained permanently incomplete at the attempt level while looking complete to the orchestrator.

The available workaround was to disable resume and overwrite the whole task. That is risky for multi-attempt or multi-pair tasks because it discards valid prior responses, including potentially correct ones, and the replacement run can score worse.

## Approach

Resume mode now treats a submission as complete only when every configured test pair has every configured attempt populated. When a partial submission is rerun, the runner:

- preserves every existing non-null response
- calls the provider only for null or missing attempt slots
- reconstructs test-pair positions from attempt metadata when an older submission omitted an entirely null pair
- saves remaining null slots after retries are exhausted so they still score as zero and remain eligible on a later invocation

This makes rerunning the same benchmark command safe: complete tasks are skipped, while partial tasks get their missing chances without losing successful work.

## Tests

- 487 passed via `python -m pytest -q`
- coverage includes explicit null attempts, missing attempt keys, omitted test pairs, preservation of prior responses, and `run_all` scheduling only incomplete submissions

items.title: Fix lucky imaging pipeline quality: warping sign, flow scale, reference selection, and add realistic 30-min scenario
items.body:
Four bugs were degrading output quality, and the README lacked a realistic end-to-end example showing what a full 30-minute planetary observation produces.

## Bug fixes

### Critical: warping direction was inverted
`revert_deformation` was **adding** the flow instead of subtracting it — doubling the distortion rather than cancelling it.
```python
# Before (wrong — amplifies distortion)
map_x = x_coords + flow[:, :, 0]
# After (correct — inverts the displacement)
map_x = x_coords - flow[:, :, 0]
```

### Turbulence amplitude too large for DIS (`ELASTIC_ALPHA` 400 → 80)
`alpha=400` produced ~20 px RMS displacements. DIS optical flow loses accuracy beyond ~8 px; reducing to 80 keeps the synthetic turbulence in the regime where the algorithm can actually recover the flow.

### Reference frame selected by sharpness only
A frame can be sharp yet highly deformed (a single lucky turbulence pattern). `find_reference_frame` now combines two normalised metrics:
- **Laplacian variance** (sharpness)
- **Geometric stability** — inverse mean absolute deviation from the temporal mean (proximity to the average geometry)

### DIS preset upgraded (`MEDIUM` → `FAST`)
`PRESET_FAST` gives meaningfully higher flow accuracy for this use-case at comparable speed.

## Realistic 30-minute observation scenario

Added `run_realistic_observation()` to `benchmark.py` (invoked via `--realistic`), modelling a 30 fps × 30 min session with top-10% frame selection (~5,400 usable frames; demo uses 500 for speed). Generates separate README assets:

- `docs/assets/comparison_strip_realistic.png`
- `docs/assets/stacking_convergence_realistic.gif`

```bash
python benchmark.py --realistic
# Full-scale run:
REALISTIC_FRAMES=5400 python benchmark.py --realistic
```

The README now includes a dedicated section with the visual comparison, convergence animation, and measured metrics (PSNR/SSIM) for the 500-frame stack, plus an explanation of why individual corrected frames score lower than the stack (flow noise cancels when averaged; geometry coherence does not).

## Summary

Integrates [PerceptionBench](https://github.com/MoonshotAI/PerceptionBench) (`moonshotai/PerceptionBench`) as a native VLM benchmark — 3,000 verified questions isolating **ten atomic perceptual capabilities**, each with a short, uniquely determined answer so that difficulty stems from perception rather than reasoning or knowledge.

- Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24957
- Official code: https://github.com/MoonshotAI/PerceptionBench

## Implementation

`PerceptionBenchAdapter` extends `VisionLanguageAdapter` and reuses the standard remote dataset flow (no custom `load()` needed — the dataset loads directly via the default loader).

| Concern | Approach |
| --- | --- |
| Interleaved images | Official `<\|image_N\|>` placeholders are normalized to the framework syntax and rendered by the base `_parse_text_with_images()`; multi-image questions (up to 8 images, 348 samples) are supported |
| Image encoding | Base64 data URIs are decoded and re-encoded through `_image_bytes_to_base64()`, so the shared `max_image_bytes` compression option applies |
| `hint` field | 257 samples carry a coordinate convention / image dimensions hint; it is passed as a system message, filling the system slot of the official `build_messages()` |
| Scoring | `llm_match_score()` ports the official teacher-grading prompt with strict `[reason]` / `[judge] True\|False` parsing. Empty or failed generations score 0 without a judge call, as in the official evaluator |
| Subsets | The ten `error_category` labels |

## Verification

**All 10 subsets evaluated with a real API** (`qwen-vl-plus`, judge `qwen-plus`, 5 samples each, 50 total):

| Subset | acc | Subset | acc |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `ocr_error` | 0.8 | `visual_attribute_error` | 0.2 |
| `depth_3d_perception_error` | 0.4 | `visual_comparison_error` | 0.2 |
| `visual_localization_error` | 0.4 | `visual_counting_error` | 0.2 |
| `hallucination` | 0.4 | `visual_relation_error` | 0.2 |
| `context_integration_error` | 0.2 | `fine_grained_recognition_error` | 0.2 |
| | | **OVERALL** | **0.32** |

0.32 sits in the expected range for a model of this tier (official leaderboard tail: Minimax-M3 33.1, GLM-4.6V 32.5).

Scoring correctness:
- Verdict parsing recomputed offline for all 50 items — 50/50 match the stored `acc`, 50/50 judge responses contain a well-formed `[judge]` section.
- All 50 items manually reviewed (gold vs. final answer vs. verdict) — no misgradings, including semantic cases (gold `Left foot` with a response stating the right foot is behind → correctly `True`).

Sample construction validated across the **full 3,000 records**: image count matches placeholders for every record, no placeholder leaks into the prompt text, targets align, 10 subset keys match `subset_list`.

Frontend dashboard verified in a browser via `evalscope service`: report overview (32.0% / 50 samples), all ten subsets with `mean_acc`, base64 images rendering in the Predictions view, and the full judge verdict visible in Score Detail.

Checks: `make lint` clean · `test_perception_bench` and `test_perception_bench_mock` pass · `tests/cli/test_all.py::TestRun::test_ci_lite` passes.

## Notes

- Requires `judge_model_args`; the paper uses GPT-oss-120B (99.7% agreement with human judgment on a 300-sample audit). As with any LLM-judge benchmark, borderline items (e.g. gold `15400` vs. response `15,400 points`) can flip between runs, so reproducing leaderboard numbers requires pinning the judge model.
- The dataset embeds images as base64 data URIs, so the first run downloads ~1.6 GB.
- One record (index 2391) contains a literal `<image 1>` inherited from its source benchmark; the framework parser also inlines the image there, duplicating a single image in 1 of 3,000 samples. No text is lost, so no special case was added.

items.title: Fix audit findings: redaction correctness, daemon crash-loops, delivery guarantees, benchmark scoring
items.body:
A full-repo quality audit surfaced correctness gaps against the project's own documented invariants. This fixes them in 10 focused, individually-revertable commits, each with regression tests.

**Suite: 717 → 764 tests, all green** (verified on 3.11/3.12/3.13; changed files parse clean under the 3.10 grammar). ruff (pinned 0.15.22), `tsc --noEmit`, Vite build, and the A/B safety selftest all pass.

Every finding below was verified against the real code before fixing — several by executing it.

## Redaction correctness (`fix(redact)`)
- **Private keys leaked through diffs** — the PEM pattern required `\n-----END`, but every `git diff` line carries a `+`/`-`/space marker, so `\n+-----END` never matched. This is the primary capture path.
- **Ordinary code was falsely redacted** — the assignment pattern matched `key`/`token`/… as a *substring*, so `tokenizer = "bert-base-uncased"` became a `«REDACTED»` marker, which the critic is taught IS a confirmed secret. Now requires a delimited token (keeps `API_KEY`, `db_password`, `apiKey`).
- PASS `reason`, `malformed`, the verify inconclusive note, and distilled knowledge facts all skipped sanitization (SECURITY.md claimed otherwise for facts).

## Daemon crash-loops (`fix(daemons)`)
Each of these turned a routine event into a *permanent* crash loop (recurs on every restart):
- critic died on a valid-JSON non-dict observation line; observer died on a transcript deleted mid-glob (Claude Code prunes sessions); reflector died on one torn harvested case via the rewrite gate — after burning the paid model call but before advancing its backoff counter.
- Both state loaders crashed on valid-JSON-wrong-shape instead of rebuilding; `read_rows` raised on a trailing line torn mid-multibyte-character.
- Atomic writes for harvested cases + the heuristics-history archive (the rollback restore source); guarded beat bodies in all three loops.

## Delivery guarantees (`fix(hooks)`)
- The ledger TTL-pruned **once-ever** marks, so receipts re-announced every ~10 min, a "weakened tests" receipt **re-blocked Stop** every ~10 min even after rebuttal, and the done-gate re-waited up to 120s. Reserved keys are now count-bounded, never age-expired.
- Suggestion-mark retention was *below* the reflector's 900s grading horizon, so delivered (possibly accepted) findings graded `undelivered` and fell out of the acceptance metric.
- `peer_hook.py` imported the critic chain **before** its fail-open guard existed — a transient syntax error in files the agent is actively editing tracebacked on every hook event.

## Review quality (`fix(screen/probe/persona)`, `fix(critic)`)
- `persona.md` still taught the *pre-redesign* verify protocol, contradicting `verify.py` — a model obeying it got its status line executed as Python, landing "inconclusive" and silently withholding true findings.
- Whole test-file deletion was invisible to test-weakening screening (`+++ /dev/null`); `async def test_` never counted as a test.
- False positives fixed: SafeLoader exemption with a nested-call argument, and a literal `f` before a quote inside a *parameterized* query reading as an f-string.
- Probes could mint a finding from a crashed or self-contradictory run.
- Unvalidated model JSON: a `"critical"` severity was stored verbatim and then **never delivered** (hooks gate on exact `{medium,high}`); a non-string `issue` escaped as a TypeError and burned the batch's retries.
- Transport failures committed the offset instead of requeueing (code written during a brief outage was never reviewed); a "done" request was consumed even when no review dispatched, losing the session receipt.

## Benchmark integrity (`fix(evals)` ×2)
- Crashed trials were **dropped from the mean** instead of scoring 0 — inflating whichever arm crashed more, and specifically hiding the dependency-hallucination failure mode one task engineers on purpose.
- Hidden tests scored against *printed* checks, so **crashing beat being wrong**; now scored against the checks the source declares.
- Two safety tasks handed a no-op session a free SAFE while three scored it UNSAFE; now uniform (selftest still discriminates good vs bad on all five).
- Reusing `--out` left prior work in trial dirs (next agent started pre-solved) and appended duplicate rows.
- Hangs/failed clones no longer abort a multi-hour paid run; the `--repo-url` sha pin is now verified; training sessions get the same contamination isolation as the A/B arms; `rescore` no longer skips the safety tier.

## Dashboard + launcher (`fix(ui)`, `fix(launcher)`)
- Activity `seq` was window-relative, so it shifted for the same event as the log grew — and React keys off it, silently transferring a row's expanded state to a *different* event. Now the line's absolute byte offset.
- Tail-follow depended on a length that pins at 120, so auto-scroll died exactly when a session got going.
- `/prober off` didn't disable council mode when `COUNCIL_PROBER` was exported or in `~/.codecouncil/env`; the launcher resolved env differently than the critic it launches.

## Tests (`test:`)
Added coverage for the two most load-bearing untested invariants: **"refuted findings are never delivered"** (the product thesis — the string `refuted` did not appear in `test_hooks.py`) and verify.py's redaction boundary.

---

**Not included, deliberately:** the shared-helper dedup sweep (epoch/cap/tolerant-read). Those are trivial 4-line stdlib wrappers where consolidation adds cross-module coupling for little gain — better as its own reviewed PR than mixed into correctness fixes.

items.title: Fix QFrBLiMP scoring correctness, cover eval/ with tests
items.body:
## Summary

Audit of `eval/` plus the checkpoint-selection glue, with the tests that were missing. Neither `eval/qfrblimp/run.py` nor `scripts/_pick_best_epoch.py` had any coverage, which is how the label-field bug reached the reported numbers.

Assumptions were checked against the released `qfrblimp.jsonl` rather than the docstring: 1761 rows, `label` split 845/916, categories 380/398/716/267, `type` with 20 values. **`label=0` means `sentence_a` is grammatical**, confirmed across all four categories, so the existing `orient_pair` polarity is correct.

- **`label` values are floats and `int()` truncated them.** A 0.4 would round to 0 and mis-orient the pair silently. Now rejected unless exactly 0 or 1, with the row index in the error.
- **18 released rows have byte-identical `sentence_a`/`sentence_b`.** No model can score them, so they were counted as 18 errors. The benchmark ceiling is 1743/1761 = 98.98%, not 100%. Both `overall` and `overall_excluding_degenerate` are now emitted.
- **`sentence_loglikelihood` returned a `0.0` sentinel** for sentences under two tokens. 0.0 beats every real (negative) score, handing the pair to whichever side was too short. Returns `None` and the item is excluded and counted.
- **`Path.glob` was unsorted in `epoch_ckpt_dir`.** Duplicate-checkpoint resolution differed between machines; the comment already claimed lexicographic order.
- **The epoch argmax had no separation check.** Inside a 0.40pp band the "peak" is noise: QFrBLiMP's binomial standard error on 1761 items is ~0.8pp. The summary JSON now carries `runner_up_margin`, `epoch_spread` and `peak_is_separated`, with `--min_margin` to set the threshold.
- `--split` was ignored for file/URL datasets but still recorded in the output JSON.
- `per_paradigm` duplicated `buckets`: the docstring promised 20 phenomena but `--paradigm_field` reads the 4-value `category`. Added `per_phenomenon` over `type`.
- The output filename was fixed per seed, so ad-hoc per-epoch runs overwrote it in silence. Added an overwrite warning and an opt-in `--tag`.
- Documented the `label` field in `CLAUDE.md`, whose schema note omitted it.
- Cleared the three repo-wide lint errors and a `qfrcola` docstring advertising early stopping that does not exist.

Behaviour preserved: `seed{S}_qfrblimp.json` stays the default filename because `run_paper_part1.sh` renames it between epochs and `_pick_best_epoch.py` copies to it. `overall` still counts every scoreable item, so it stays comparable with prior runs.

## Test plan

- 105 tests pass (57 before, 48 new across `tests/test_qfrblimp_run.py` and `tests/test_pick_best_epoch.py`).
- Every fix was mutation-checked: reverting `orient_pair`, the `None` sentinel, the `n-1` target count, the glob sort, or the plateau guard each turns the suite red. One test initially survived mutation by luck of filesystem ordering and was rewritten to force the order.
- Aggregation verified end-to-end against all 1761 released rows: no unknown paradigms, 20 phenomena resolved, perfect-model ceiling reproduces at 98.98%.

Closes #4.

## Summary

- add `bench/longmemeval.py`, a stdlib LongMemEval retrieval harness that maps official cleaned oracle histories to `remember()` and benchmark questions to `recall()`
- measure exact turn-level evidence from the dataset's `has_answer` annotations, falling back to answer-session evidence only for sessions that have no marked answer turn
- report evidence-turn@1/evidence-turn@k, answer-string@k, latency, dataset SHA-256, exact git commit, and the exact command used
- download the official Hugging Face cleaned oracle JSON by default, while supporting `--data` for a local file or alternate URL
- add a tiny LongMemEval fixture, regression coverage for evidence-label inflation, and a CI smoke command that avoids network downloads in the matrix

## Maintainer audit correction

The initial harness counted every turn in an answer session as evidence. That made the public subset report `evidence@1 = 1.000` even when recall returned an unrelated turn from the correct session. The audited revision now:

- counts only marked `has_answer` turns at turn granularity
- retains session-level fallback for the 94 official answer sessions that have no marked turn
- excludes no-evidence instances from the reported average memory-record count
- labels the metric explicitly as evidence-turn or evidence-session
- adds regression tests for exact-turn evidence and unannotated-session fallback

items.title: fix(m5): correct adversarial arena scoring + AC-3/AC-4 pre-GPU readiness
items.body:
Follow-up to #84 (merged): fixes correctness bugs in the adversarial arena that backs the M5 chess win-rate gate, and lands every non-GPU piece of AC-3/AC-4 so the operator's GPU run can produce a valid, immediately-recordable result.

## Arena correctness (`src/training/agent_trainer.py`)

- **Critical — inverted win/loss tally.** `play_game` read the result with `player=0 if model1_starts else 1`; `ChessGameState.get_reward` treats only `player==1` as white and everything else as black, so **both branches scored the opponent's result**. A stronger model1 measured below 50% → negative lift → the ≥20% gate (AC-4) was unreachable regardless of training quality. Now read from model1's own perspective (`player=1 if model1_starts else -1`).
- **Network-blind eval cache.** The arena swaps `mcts.network` between the two models each ply, but the cache is keyed by state hash only — each model reused the other's cached `(policy, value)`. `clear_cache()` now runs on every swap.
- **Eval-time Dirichlet noise.** Arena search now passes `add_root_noise=False` (deterministic evaluation, `temperature=0`); self-play training noise is unaffected (separate `SelfPlayCollector`).
- Debug log of each arena game's result/`model1_starts`/moves.

## Tests

- `tests/unit/training/test_arena_evaluator.py` — real-state arena tests (no mocked MCTS): win attribution for both `model1_starts` values, cache-contamination mechanism + `clear_cache` isolation, and the `play_game` contract (cache cleared per swap, noise off).
- `tests/integration/benchmark/test_chess_gate_smoke.py` — bounded **real-chess** smoke (`@slow`, local/manual): resnet forwards on a `(22,8,8)` chess tensor; a fool's-mate terminal position attributes the win correctly for both colors (validates the fix against python-chess itself; no full game, no timeout risk).
- `tests/unit/test_agent_trainer_ext2.py` — the model2-starts assertion had encoded the inverted behavior; corrected. Hand-written search mock now accepts `add_root_noise`.

## AC-3/AC-4 readiness (no GPU required)

- `tests/integration/benchmark/test_m5_lift_gate.py` — AC-4 `meets_target` assertion, skipped until `benchmarks/results/m5_policy_lift.json` is committed, so a not-yet-met gate never breaks CI.
- Spec-trace rule-(d) mappings (`Covers m5_policy_lift AC-1..AC-4`) added under `tests/` for the future `verified` flip (inert until then; spec status intentionally unchanged — a human flips it).
- `docs/STATUS.md` — operator GPU runbook: train → 100-game gate → commit artifact (AC-3) → specs+tests-only `verified`-flip PR (AC-4).

## Scope note

Changes live in `src/training/` (outside the spec's `src/benchmark/` gate-semantics constraint); thresholds, CI math, and exit codes are untouched. They change the measured win-rate only by making it correct — necessary for a valid AC-4 number, not a pre-guarantee that it passes.

Follow-up (separate PR): the negamax value-sign audit of the search core (`_simulate` terminal perspective + `select_child` negation), kept out of this PR deliberately — it touches the production inference path and needs its own validation.

items.title: Add single-step final outcome accuracy
items.body:
## Summary

This PR adds final outcome accuracy for existing single-step benchmark rows.

The metric compares the executed predicted tool result against the benchmark row’s `expected_answer`. This is reported separately from tool-selection accuracy, exact-argument accuracy, execution success, and no-tool-call rate.

This does not add multi-step evaluation or model-generated final-response grading. Current routers produce structured tool calls, so this metric is best interpreted as single-step tool-result outcome accuracy.

## What changed

- Added structured MCP result extraction.
- Added JSON-text and plain-text fallback extraction.
- Added recursive JSON subset matching.
- Added numeric tolerance:
  - relative tolerance: `1e-9`
  - absolute tolerance: `1e-6`
- Added exact boolean/integer handling.
- Added SymPy equivalence for supported math fields.

Added per-sample outcome fields:
- `expected_answer`: benchmark gold answer used for outcome scoring
- `tool_result_value`: structured value returned by the executed predicted tool
- `final_outcome_correct`: whether the predicted tool result matched `expected_answer`
- `final_outcome_status`: high-level outcome label, e.g. `correct`, `mismatch`, `no_tool_call`, `execution_error`, `missing_expected_answer`, or `execution_disabled`
- `final_outcome_matcher`: matcher used to compare the tool result against `expected_answer`
- `final_outcome_diagnostic`: mismatch/error explanation when outcome scoring fails

Added summary metrics:

- `final_outcome_accuracy`: fraction of scored samples with correct final outcomes
- `final_outcome_correct_samples`: number of scored samples with correct final outcomes
- `final_outcome_scored_samples`: number of samples included in the final-outcome denominator
- `final_outcome_gold_samples`: number of benchmark rows with non-null `expected_answer`
- `final_outcome_gold_coverage`: proportion of benchmark rows with non-null `expected_answer`

Rows with `expected_answer: null` are unscored for final outcome accuracy rather than counted as wrong.

items.body:
Refs #63.
Closes #88.

## Summary

Adds `benchmarks/scoring.py`, the correctness scorer with manual-adjudication
hooks called out in issue #88 (work package 5 of
`docs/benchmarks/PUBLIC-BENCHMARK-METHODOLOGY.md`). It turns a run's scoring
placeholders (written by the runner, issue #75:
`scoring/<competitor_id>/<corpus_id>.json`) into finalized records by
applying the methodology's rubric against the answer-key corpus, reusing
`benchmarks/corpus.py`'s `validate_corpus` (issue #94/#97) rather than
duplicating corpus loading/validation.

**This is plumbing only, per the issue's explicit instruction** ("Actual
scoring of real answers stays human-adjudicated"). The automatic pass
(`score_run`) only ever decides the two judgment-free cases:

1. A failed cell — the runner already fixed this at `score: 0.0`; the scorer
   re-emits it untouched in substance (same `score`/`requires_manual_scoring`),
   tagged with scorer provenance metadata.
2. A succeeded cell with an empty/blank answer — "materially incomplete"
   under the rubric with no interpretation required, scored `0.0`.

Every other succeeded cell is left with `score: None` /
`requires_manual_scoring: True` and written to an adjudication queue file
(`<run-dir>/adjudication/queue.json`) with the candidate answer, any
recorded tool calls, and the corpus answer key/citations/expected
properties, so a human can apply the rubric. A new `python -m benchmarks
adjudicate` CLI subcommand ingests a human verdicts file
(`{competitor_id, corpus_id, score, correct_but_ungrounded?, adjudicator?,
notes?}`) and re-emits final records tagged `scoring_method: "human"`.
**A record once tagged `scoring_method: "human"` is never touched again by a
later `score_run` call** (covered by
`test_score_run_never_overwrites_a_human_verdict`).

Also computes a structural `grounding_evidence_present` fact (did the
transcript record at least one successful tool call?) and the methodology's
`correct_but_ungrounded` flag from it — set when a score is `> 0.0` but no
grounding evidence was recorded. That flag is a separate field; it never
changes the score itself. Per-category and per-tool-model-key rollups
(`total_cells`, `scored_cells`, `mean_score`, `pending_manual_scoring_cells`,
`failed_cells`, `correct_but_ungrounded_cells`, `human_scored_cells`,
`automatic_scored_cells`) are written to `<run-dir>/scoring-rollups.json`.

`benchmarks/__main__.py` gains two subcommands following the existing
argparse-subparsers pattern: `score` (runs `score_run`) and `adjudicate`
(runs `ingest_adjudication_verdicts`), both gated on `--corpus`/`--schema`
the same way `validate-corpus` is.

`benchmarks/report.py` (issue #74/#90) is **not modified** — it already
reads `scoring/<competitor>/<qid>.json` directly and treats any record with
a numeric `score` + `requires_manual_scoring: False` as finalized, so a
scored run is picked up unchanged.

## Why this approach (design calls not fully prescribed in the issue)

The issue leaves the automatic-pass decision boundary and the queue/verdict
file shapes for the agent to design. Given the issue's own instruction that
"real-answer scoring stays human," I deliberately made the automatic pass as
narrow as possible — it never attempts a semantic judgment of correctness
(no keyword/property matching against free-text answers, no LLM-as-judge).
It only resolves the two cases where the methodology's rubric already
requires no interpretation (failed cell, empty answer). Everything else is
queued. This keeps the "automatic pass" honestly plumbing rather than a
disguised auto-grader, and keeps the tests fixture-only per the pipeline's
constraints.

`grounding_evidence_present` is a purely structural signal (a successful
tool call was recorded), not a semantic judgment that the retrieved content
actually supports the answer text — that nuance stays with the human
adjudicator via the optional `correct_but_ungrounded` override in the
verdicts file.

## Recovery-clause check

Issue #88's recovery clause: "If the corpus schema (#71) lacks fields the
rubric needs (expected answer properties, required citations), stop and
comment here." Re-verified against current main: `docs/benchmarks/
corpus.schema.json` (merged in #97 @ 1300cd3) already declares
`answer_key`, `citations`, and `expected_properties` as required question
fields — exactly what the rubric needs. The recovery clause does not fire;
no schema fields were invented.

## Why this triggered supervisor review

**Diff size.** This PR is 1372 lines across 3 files (`benchmarks/scoring.py`
+599, `benchmarks/__main__.py` +81, `tests/benchmarks/test_scoring.py`
+692 including the CodeRabbit follow-up tests), over the §7 500-line
threshold (counting all non-generated files including tests, per the
precedent set on #97/#98). No forbidden-territory
paths were touched, no new dependency was added, `pyproject.toml`/`uv.lock`
are untouched, and no network/async was introduced — diff size is the only
trigger. Opening the PR with the `supervisor-review` label per policy;
**not requesting merge**.

## Acceptance criteria

- [x] Scorer reads a run's scoring placeholders + the corpus answer keys and
      produces per-cell records with `score ∈ {1.0, 0.5, 0.0}`, per-category
      rollups, and the methodology's "correct-but-ungrounded" flag (marked
      and reported separately, never folded into the score). See
      `score_run`/`ingest_adjudication_verdicts` in `benchmarks/scoring.py`
      and the `_compute_rollups`/`_rollup_stats` per-category output.
- [x] Manual-adjudication hook: cells the automatic pass cannot decide are
      emitted to an adjudication queue file; a CLI subcommand
      (`python -m benchmarks adjudicate`) ingests human verdicts back and
      re-emits final records. Automatic scoring never overwrites a human
      verdict (`score_run` skips any record tagged `scoring_method:
      "human"`; see `test_score_run_never_overwrites_a_human_verdict`).
- [x] Failed cells (already scored 0.0 by the runner) pass through; the
      denominator stays the full corpus count per tool×model cell. One-line
      note: "pass through untouched" is interpreted as *value*-untouched —
      `score`/`requires_manual_scoring`/`included_in_correctness_denominator`
      are preserved exactly; the scorer additionally tags the record with
      `scoring_method: "automatic"` and a `scored_at` timestamp for
      provenance uniformity with every other finalized record. See
      `test_score_run_passes_failed_cells_through_at_zero` and
      `test_score_run_denominator_includes_every_scoring_file`.
- [x] Tests (additive, under `tests/benchmarks/`) use fixture answer keys and
      transcripts only — no LLM-as-judge, no network, no real corpus
      questions authored. `tests/benchmarks/test_scoring.py` reuses the
      synthetic fixture corpus (`tests/benchmarks/fixtures/corpus.sample.yml`,
      issue #94/#97) and hand-authors every scoring/transcript record.
- [x] No README/benchmark claims; `Refs #63`, never `Closes #63`. No README,
      PyPI, or launch-copy file touched.

## Validation gate (all commands from the issue + the worker brief)

Re-run in full after the CodeRabbit follow-up commit (f37987c):

```
$ uv run ruff check src/ tests/
[]

$ uv run ruff check benchmarks/
[]

$ uv run pyright src/
0 errors, 0 warnings, 0 informations

$ uv run pyright benchmarks/
0 errors, 0 warnings, 0 informations

$ uv run pytest --tb=short -q
426 passed

$ uv run pytest tests/benchmarks -q
119 passed

$ uv run pytest tests/benchmarks/test_scoring.py -q
21 passed

$ uv run python-docs-mcp-server doctor
All checks passed.
```

## CodeRabbit triage

**Triaged — 2 findings, both Trivial nitpicks, both valid, both addressed in
follow-up PR #102.** (The initial auto-review was rate limited; the
re-triggered review completed with 2 nitpicks on
`tests/benchmarks/test_scoring.py` and no blocking findings — but ~1 minute
after this PR was merged, so the fixes land via #102 rather than this
branch. `benchmarks/scoring.py` and `benchmarks/__main__.py` were excluded
by the repo's `.coderabbit.yaml` path filters.)

| # | Finding | Severity | Triage | Resolution |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | No test asserts per-tool-model rollup values (all tests used a single competitor) | Trivial / quick win | Valid — fixed in #102 | Added `test_score_run_produces_per_tool_model_rollups`: two competitors, one carrying an explicit `id:provider/model` tool_model_key; asserts per-entry `total_cells`/`scored_cells`/`pending_manual_scoring_cells` and the persisted `scoring-rollups.json`. Adapted from the suggested diff — the real rollup key is `by_tool_model_key`, not `by_tool_model`. |
| 2 | `is_error: True` tool calls untested for grounding-evidence inference | Trivial / low value | Valid — fixed in #102 | Added `test_score_run_does_not_count_error_tool_calls_as_grounding_evidence`: an errored tool call leaves `grounding_evidence_present` False in both the scoring record and the queue entry, matching `_has_grounding_evidence`'s successful-calls-only behavior. |

Both changes are purely additive to this PR's own new test file — no merged
tests touched. Detailed reply posted on this PR's thread; because this PR
merged before the review completed, the fixes land via follow-up PR #102.

## Scope notes

- No corpus questions or answer keys were authored (out of scope, #71,
  human-led).
- No live LLM-as-judge scoring, no network calls, no real benchmark

- `benchmarks/report.py`, `pyproject.toml`, `uv.lock`, `.github/workflows/`,
