items.title: feat(tasks): add AdvancedIF rubric-graded instruction-following benchmark
items.body:
## Type

- feature — new benchmark, task, or capability

## Summary

- Adds **AdvancedIF** (Meta, [arXiv:2511.10507](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.10507), upstream [facebookresearch/AdvancedIF](https://github.com/facebookresearch/AdvancedIF/blob/f9d30137c4139d4d9af260ae28108b5afae828c0/judge.py)): 1,645 expert-written prompts with human-curated rubrics across complex single-turn (402), system steerability (507) and carried-context multi-turn (736) instruction following. A grader LLM answers every rubric question; headline `score` = overall pass rate, with the co-published `micro_pass_rate` and a per-aspect breakdown.
- **The judge prompts are not vendored.** Upstream ships *every* file under CC-BY-NC-4.0 (LICENSE file, not just the README), which cannot be redistributed inside this Apache-2.0 tree — there is currently no NC-licensed code in `sieval/`, only NC `license=` metadata on dataset pointers. The operator stages their own checkout and points `SIEVAL_ADVANCED_IF_SRC` at it; the loader sha256-pins `judge.py` to `f9d3013` and refuses a drifted revision. The data is CC-BY-NC-4.0 too and likewise only referenced, so running this benchmark accepts the upstream terms either way. Side benefit: the prompts are byte-exact by construction rather than by review.
- **Reproduces an upstream defect on purpose.** Upstream selects the system-steerability judge on `benchmark_name == "if_system_steerability_oss"`, a value the released dataset never contains (it ships `system_steerability_v2`) — so all 507 system-prompt rows are graded by the plain user-instruction judge, and the CLI's `--task` choices match zero rows. `processor.process_file`'s own docstring uses the released spelling, so the `if_*_oss` literals are what went stale. Per `sieval/tasks/CLAUDE.md`, the unqualified name tracks upstream including defects. **The delta is now measured: +0.00** (Validation §5), so there is no `_fixed` variant to ship — an unmeasured fork is not a fix, and a measured-at-zero fork is not one either. A test pins the behaviour so it cannot be "cleaned up" silently.
- **The two published rates deliberately do not share a denominator**: the per-sample rubric rate divides by the rubric count the *data* carries, while the pooled `micro_pass_rate` counts every answer key the *grader* emitted. Both are kept, each matching its own upstream definition, with the raw counts a pooled rate cannot reconstruct persisted per rollout.
- The whole rubric goes to the grader in **one indexed call per rollout**, so its `ModelOutput` is stored as a single mapping and its spend reaches `profile.json` (`iter_grader_outputs` skips a list). Verified on a real run: the `feedback` stage reports 3,788,113 input / 159,316 output tokens over 1,644 rollouts.
- `status="experimental"` — the port is now **verified correct** (Validation §1–§3), but no published number is reproducible: the paper's judge (`o3-mini-2025-01-31`) and every model it evaluates are legacy or retired, and judge choice alone is worth **~29 points** on this metric (§4). See "Why this stays experimental".

## Test Plan

### Automated

- [x] Lint/format clean (`ruff check && ruff format --check` — clean across `sieval/` and `tests/`)
- [x] Type check clean (`ty check` clean; `mypy --strict` emits only the same pre-existing `no-untyped-def`/`type-arg` classes as the sibling grader task `simpleqa_verified_0shot_gen`)
- [x] Unit tests pass (3215 passed, 44 new)

Also clean: `scripts/check_preflight.py` (all checks, no FAIL/WARN), and `sync_meta_index.py --check` / `sync_package_stubs.py --check`.

### Manual

- [x] **Real upstream prompts, end to end (offline).** Staged a checkout at the pinned commit; the sha256 gate passes, `judge.py` imports, and both judge prompts compose with every slot filled (`judge_prompt` 1,048 chars; system-steer 28,587 chars incl. the 27,227-char few-shot block). A realistic grader reply then parses and scores correctly. The 27KB few-shot block is also the concrete reason vendoring was not an option.
- [x] **Real dataset at the pinned revision.** `sieval dataset download advanced_if` succeeds and `sieval task show advanced_if_0shot_gen` reports `Ready: yes`. Loaded rows match the modelled schema exactly: 1,645 rows, three `str` columns, `train` mirrored to `test`, and `benchmark_name` counts 402 / 507 / 736 as documented.

## Validation

Added after the original submission. **§1–§3 are model-free and require no API spend**; §4–§5 are live runs.

### 1. Differential test against upstream's own code

Upstream's `judge.py` / `processor.py` imported and executed unmodified, with only `_call_openai_api` stubbed to return a canned reply — so every parsing, counting and pooling rule under test is upstream's real code.

| Claim | Scope | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Judge prompt byte-identical to upstream `_compose_prompt` | all 1,645 rows, **both** judge classes | **0 mismatches** |
| Routing predicate identical (`is_system_steer`) | all 1,645 rows | **0 mismatches** |
| Per-row verdict identical (`satisfied_all` + `rubric_level_pass_rate`) | 21,385 (row, reply) pairs, 13 reply shapes | **0 mismatches** |
| Pooled `overall_pass_rate` / `micro_pass_rate` identical | 19,740 pairs, 12 schema-conforming shapes | **exact to 1e-9** |

Reply shapes include over-indexed `question_N` keys, partial key sets, missing declaration, missing/non-mapping `rubrics_check`, `question_foo`, `" yes "` padding, non-JSON prose and empty. The prompt check also covers the judge the routing defect strands.

**One divergence, localised.** `nonstring_answer` (a rubric answer arriving as `true`, not `"Yes"`) — the documented deviation. It moves **only `micro_pass_rate`** (sieval adds the check to the pooled denominator; upstream fails the whole row). Per-row verdicts and the headline `overall_pass_rate` are unaffected, and it never fired in 1,644 live gradings.

### 2. Paper Table 1 reproduced exactly

Reproducing the published dataset statistics from this PR's own loaders tests `parse_rubrics` / `parse_conversation` against numbers the authors published — the rubric field is sometimes double-JSON-encoded, so avg-criteria landing on 7.44 is a real check.

| Category | n | paper | avg criteria | paper | avg turns | paper |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Explicit and Complex IF | 402 | 402 | 7.44 | 7.44 | 1.00 | 1.00 |
| Multi-turn Carried Context IF | 736 | 736 | 6.08 | 6.08 | 7.69 | 7.69 |
| System Prompt Steerability | 507 | 507 | 9.81 | 9.81 | 11.21 | 11.21 |

Total 1,645 = paper Table 2. **All 9 cells match** ⇒ the pinned revision is the population the paper evaluated. ("Turns" counts every message in the dialog, system turn included — the only reading that lands all three averages at once.)

### 3. Live run health

Full 1,645 rows, `gpt-5.1` @ `reasoning_effort=high`, one grader call per rollout.

- 1,644/1,645 graded (one `APITimeoutError` at infer, not retried).
- **0** grader parse failures, **0** truncated responses (all finish `stop`), **0** empty responses.
- Grader self-consistent: declared-YES 779 vs all-rubrics-YES 790 (23 / 12 disagreements each way).
- `n_rubric_checks` 12,448 ≈ 1,644 × 7.6; per-aspect keys populate correctly.

### 4. Score comparison — and why it is not a reproduction

Paper Table 3, GPT-5 "Thinking": CIF 86.9 / CC 73.9 / SS 72.8 / avg 77.9. Every row below re-grades the **same stored responses** on the **same 450 rows** (150/aspect), so only the judge varies. Model under test is `gpt-5.1` throughout (the paper's GPT-5 is not available).

| judge | CIF | CC | SS | avg | vs paper | tok/call | full-1,644 judging cost |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| gpt-5.4-mini, default effort | 52.0 | 47.3 | 44.7 | 48.0 | −29.9 | ~2,400 | 3.79M (measured) |
| gpt-5.4-mini, `effort=high` | 80.7 | 60.7 | 54.0 | 65.1 | −12.8 | — | — |
| gemini-3-flash-preview, `thinking=high` | 88.0 | 67.3 | 58.0 | 71.1 | −6.8 | 5,584 | 8.92M |
| gemini-3.1-pro-preview, `thinking=low` | 92.0 | 74.0 | 64.0 | **76.7** | **−1.2** | 3,086 | 5.07M |

**−1.2 on the macro is NOT a reproduction.** The per-aspect errors merely cancel:

| judge | CIF | CC | SS | macro |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| gemini-3.1-pro `low` | **+5.1** | +0.1 | **−8.8** | −1.2 |
| gemini-3-flash `high` | +1.1 | −6.6 | −14.8 | −6.8 |
| gpt-5.4-mini `high` | −6.2 | −13.2 | −18.8 | −12.8 |

A genuine reproduction matches **per aspect**, not just in the average. Two substitutions remain uncontrolled (model and judge), and per-sample agreement between the two best judges is only 61.8%. Do not quote 76.7 as agreement with the paper.

**How much of the spread is the judge.** All on identical rows:

- **Judge reasoning effort: +17.1** (48.0 → 65.1, same model / responses / prompts, only the effort knob). The default-effort grader emitted 0-character reasoning traces and ~97 output tokens for up to 20 rubrics, while the model under test spent ~2,900 per answer — badly under-powered against a reasoning judge like o3-mini.
- **Judge capability: +11.6** (65.1 → 76.7).
- ⇒ **judge choice spans ~29 points**, nearly the entire original gap.

**Why so sensitive: the metric amplifies judge noise.** The headline is all-or-nothing over ~7.6 criteria. Raising judge effort moved per-rubric `micro` only 87.2 → 91.8 (+4.6) but all-pass +17.1 — a **3.4× amplification**. Judge instability at the per-prompt level, measured: **86.6%** self-agreement (same judge, same config, re-run), 69.1% across effort settings, 61.8% across families. Aggregate stability hides per-prompt churn, and all-or-nothing multiplies the churn. The paper measures the same fragility from the other side (its Table 4, per-rubric F1 vs human experts: o3-mini 0.723, vanilla Llama 4 Maverick 0.515).

**Judge cost note.** A flagship judge at *low* thinking is both the best and the cheapest option here: `gemini-3.1-pro` `thinking=low` vs `thinking=high` was indistinguishable in quality (68.9 vs 66.7 on 45 rows, one sample apart) while `high` cost +38% tokens and 2× latency. It thinks ~400–460 tokens/call against gemini-3-flash's 2,851 at `thinking=high`. Budget for a real judge: grading cost is the same order as generating the answers (5.07M vs 6.97M here).

**Reproduced qualitatively:** the paper's stated finding that single-turn complex IF scores above multi-turn and system steerability — CIF > CC and CIF > SS holds under **every** judge arm.

### 5. Upstream routing defect — measured delta

All 507 SS rows, same responses, same judge (`gpt-5.4-mini` `effort=high`), only the judge prompt changes (5,893 → 31,598 chars, the difference being the 27KB few-shot block):

| routing | SS pass rate | per-rubric micro |
| --- | --- | --- |
| upstream's actual (plain user-instruction judge) | 52.07 | 90.81 |
| intended (system-steer judge) | 52.07 | 91.27 |
| **delta** | **+0.00** | +0.46 |

**Score-neutral in aggregate**, while churning **13.8%** of individual verdicts (35 fail→pass, 35 pass→fail; the exact cancellation is coincidence — micro moving +0.46 confirms the two arms really saw different prompts). This also refutes the natural hypothesis that mis-routing is why SS lags the paper most: it is not. SS carries the most criteria per dialog (9.81 vs 7.44 / 6.08), so the all-or-nothing rule penalises it hardest.

Consequence: **no `_fixed` variant.** It would still matter for per-sample analysis, since 1 row in 7 changes verdict.

## Why this stays `experimental`

The blocker is not effort — it is that **the reproduction target has expired**:

- The paper's judge is `o3-mini-2025-01-31` (Jan 2025); the models it evaluates are GPT-5, GPT-4.1, Gemini 2.5/3 Pro, Claude 4 Sonnet, Llama 4 Maverick. All are superseded or retired.
- Judge choice moves this metric ~29 points, so a comparison table without the original judge reports mostly a judge result.
- Upstream ships no calibration set. The paper *has* human-labeled rubric judgments (its Table 4) but does not release them, so a replacement judge cannot be validated against human agreement before use.

The `Score comparison table` checklist item is therefore **unsatisfiable by construction** for this benchmark, not merely pending. What §1–§3 provide instead is the durable substitute: a differential test against upstream's code, the published dataset statistics reproduced exactly, and a live reference point with the judge pinned plus a measured self-replay noise floor — enough to make future runs comparable **to each other** even when they cannot be compared to the paper.

Promoting to `stable` would require either access to the original judge, or a decision that the above substitute is the accepted bar for judge-dependent benchmarks whose judge has aged out.

## Follow-ups (not in this PR)

- `reference_impl.notes` describes the grader as "temperature 0". **Upstream never sends temperature** — `judge.py` stores `self.temperature` but `_call_openai_api` passes only `max_completion_tokens` and `response_format`. Following the note literally makes every call fail on a reasoning-model grader (`"temperature, top_p and n are fixed at 1"`), o3-mini included, which is presumably why upstream drops it. One clause to fix, and it matters: a fully-failed grading stage still reports `score: 0.0`, which reads as a score rather than a floor.
- The `nonstring_answer` deviation should say **which** metric it moves (`micro_pass_rate` only, §1).
- `VALIDATION: none` in `reference_impl.notes` should be replaced by a pointer to §1–§4 and the judge-expiry caveat.

## Checklist

### Required (all PRs)

- [x] PR title follows conventional format (`type(scope): description`)
- [x] No internal paths, credentials, or personal info in committed files
- [x] AI-generated code has `AI-Generated Code - <model> (<provider>)` in module docstring
- [x] No new upper-layer dependencies added to `core/`
- [x] Deleted code verified — no remaining call sites depend on it (nothing deleted; additive only)

### If: New or Modified Benchmark

- [x] Reference paper/repo linked in Summary
- [ ] Score comparison table included — Validation §4 has the table and the per-aspect diff; it is **not** a reproduction, and cannot be one (see "Why this stays `experimental`")
- [x] Dataset loading tested (`sieval dataset download advanced_if` succeeds)
- [x] Task registered in package-level `__init__.py` (lazy auto-discovering registry; `__init__.pyi` stubs + `meta/index.json` regenerated, and name resolution verified via `sieval task show`)

### If: community/ Changes

- [x] Upstream diff documented — module docstring of `sieval/community/advanced_if.py` enumerates the reproduced routing defect plus two deviations: a fenced-JSON parse fallback (sieval cannot force `response_format=json_object` on an arbitrary grader endpoint the way upstream's OpenAI client does — without it a grader that fences its JSON would score zero everywhere, a harness artifact rather than a model property), and stringifying non-string rubric answers instead of aborting the row. The fallback earned its keep: the `gemini-3.1-pro` / `gemini-3-flash` arms in §4 reach the gateway through a protocol shim that drops `response_format`, and still produced 0 unparsed replies across 450 gradings.
- [x] License attribution preserved — upstream commit-pinned permalink and the CC-BY-NC-4.0 terms are stated in the module header, the dataset `license=` field, and the task's `reference_impl.notes`.

## Running it

```bash
git clone https://github.com/facebookresearch/AdvancedIF && \
  git -C AdvancedIF checkout f9d30137c4139d4d9af260ae28108b5afae828c0
export SIEVAL_ADVANCED_IF_SRC=$PWD/AdvancedIF
sieval dataset download advanced_if
```

Then pass `grader:` in the task args. Upstream's own request shape is
`max_completion_tokens=32768` + `response_format={"type": "json_object"}` and
**no `temperature`** — it stores one but never sends it, and reasoning-model
graders reject an explicit value. Give the judge a real thinking budget: at
default effort the same judge scored 29 points lower (§4).

```yaml
    args:
      grader:
        model: <a reasoning-capable judge>
        api_base: ...
        max_completion_tokens: 32768
        response_format: {type: json_object}
        # reasoning_effort / thinking level: set it explicitly
```

items.title: perf: benchmark the worst case, not the worst shape
items.body:
R10 / RB-04. The published p95 described the maximum input *shape*. This measures the maximum NLI *work*, and the result misses the p95 hard limit in every run and sits directly on the measurement deadline.

## What the reference workload actually measures

`reference.json` submits 5 candidates x 4 claims = 160 cross-candidate pairs, and its claims are about four different subjects. E1 correctly drops 100 of those pairs as not comparable, so **60 reach the NLI model**. The published 3,468 ms p95 is a real measurement of 60 pairs of inference, against a contract that permits 160.

README and `docs/performance.md` both called that workload "the maximum legal one ... every same-scope pair scored in both directions". Both are corrected here.

## The adversarial workload

`benchmarks/workloads/adversarial.json` puts all five candidates on one subject and one scope. Measured, not assumed:

| | value |
|---|---|
| cross pairs | 160 |
| relevant after E1 | **160** (lowest similarity 0.7222 against a 0.42 floor) |
| scope divergent | 0 |
| contradiction denominator | **160** |
| scored by NLI, both directions | **160** (320 calls) |

`run.py` asserts all of that and fails the run if E1 removes a single pair. `pairs_scored_by_nli` is the witness for bidirectionality: a pair counts as scored only when both `score_a_to_b` and `score_b_to_a` exist.

## What it costs — two release runs, back to back, idle machine

| Metric | Idle run A | Idle run B | Reference (worst of 3) | Target | Hard limit |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Pairs scored by NLI | 160 of 160 | 160 of 160 | 60 of 160 | — | — |
| Preflight p95 | 0.144 ms | 0.110 ms | 0.150 ms | < 15 ms | < 50 ms |
| Measurement p50 | 8,395 ms | 8,529 ms | 3,232 ms | — | — |
| Measurement p95 | **9,421 ms** | **9,985 ms** | 3,468 ms | < 3,500 ms | **< 8,000 ms** |
| Measurement p99 | 9,564 ms | **10,246 ms** | 3,579 ms | < 9,000 ms | **< 10,000 ms** |
| CPU per measurement | 18.79 s | 19.31 s | 6.59 s | — | — |
| Peak RSS | 953 MB | 953 MB | 750 MB | < 2.2 GB | < 3 GB |
| Default report size | 3,205 B | 3,205 B | 3,175 B | < 6 KB | < 12 KB |
| Cold start | 11,549 ms | 10,800 ms | 5,748 ms | reported | not gated |
| Deadline verdict | PASS (exit 0) | **FAIL (exit 1)** | PASS | — | 10 s |

**The 8,000 ms p95 hard limit is missed in both runs, by 18% and 25%.** The two runs agree to within 1.6% on p50, 2.8% on CPU-seconds and 20 KB on peak RSS — and disagree on the verdict. Run A's worst measurement took 9,564 ms and passed; run B's took 10,246 ms and failed, which is also 2.5% over the 10,000 ms p99 hard limit. Whether the legal-maximum workload completes is decided by the run, not by the input. That is a worse property than a clean failure, because it passes in CI and times out on a user's machine.

### Under load

A third run of the identical workload, taken while the machine was busy, measured p95 14,340 ms, p99 14,592 ms and 30.96 CPU-seconds, and `service.measure()` returned a typed `TIMEOUT` rather than a report — verified directly against the shipped 10 s deadline, not inferred. It is reported separately and **not** folded into the range above: ambient load moves this workload by roughly 50% against a margin of 4%.

The tell is the preflight column. Preflight is pure Python and loads no model, so its p95 tripling from 0.110–0.144 ms to 0.306 ms measured the machine, not the code. An earlier revision of this PR published the loaded run as the headline worst case; that was wrong, and the load check is now documented so the mistake is catchable next time.

## Peak RSS

`peak_rss_bytes` was a single `process.memory_info().rss` reading taken after the last measurement returned. That is not a peak — the maximum sits inside a measurement. It is now a maximum sampled across the process tree every 50 ms on a background thread, with the end-of-run reading kept beside it as `rss_sampling.final_rss_bytes` for comparison.

Every reading now goes through `PeakRssSampler.sample()`, which folds it into the maximum before returning it. Taken outside the maximum, that final reading came back **4 KB above the recorded peak** on a real run — a peak smaller than a number published next to it is not a peak. It also covers the same process tree the sampler does, so the pair differs only in *when* it was sampled, never in *what* was counted.

## What did NOT change

No threshold moved. The 8,000 ms budget, the 10 s deadline, `MAX_CROSS_CANDIDATE_PAIRS`, and the fixed 2-thread inference settings are untouched. The regression baseline has **not** been re-pinned — three consecutive runs on an idle machine are what a baseline requires, and a workload that straddles its own deadline is not something to pin a regression budget to before that has been ruled on. R10's re-baseline bullet stays open, with the reason recorded in `docs/performance.md`.

## Verification

- Suite: `557 passed, 2 deselected`, exit 0 (baseline on `main` was 551; six new controls).
- `scripts/release_gate.py --text`: `verdict: PASS  blocking: 0`, one SKIP (G15, by design).
- mypy `Success: no issues found in 76 source files`; ruff format and check clean.
- Six new controls in the mutation suite, run by name: the assertion accepts the full pair space, rejects the reference workload's real 60-pair coverage, rejects a pair scored in one direction only, rejects a scope-divergent pair; the sampler records a maximum a final reading would miss; and a reading taken beside the peak can never exceed it.
- Benchmark output validated key-by-key against `report_schema.json`: no missing required fields, no undeclared keys, in all three new blocks.

Addresses both CodeRabbit findings: `pair_work` is now `required` (and the unreachable `report is not None` guard that justified it being optional is gone), and `final_rss_bytes` reads the same process tree as the peak.

  * Benchmark reports now include deadline results, pair-coverage metrics, sampled process-tree peak memory, and clearer failure diagnostics.
  * Benchmark execution now detects incomplete scoring, missed deadlines, and adversarial workload failures.

* **Documentation**
  * Expanded performance documentation with reference and adversarial workload results, including timing, CPU, memory, and timeout details.
  * Clarified benchmark limitations and updated published performance figures.

* **Tests**
  * Added coverage for pair completeness, bidirectional scoring, scope validation, and peak memory sampling.

items.title: feat: compare two system versions against a benchmark dataset (US4)
items.body:
## Summary
Implements User Story 4 (P2, admin/evaluator only): maintain a benchmark dataset of question/expected-answer pairs, run two named system versions against it, and get per-question and aggregate correctness/relevance/groundedness scores with a declared winner. Regular users are rejected with 403.

Three commits, one per subphase:
1. **Tests** — contract tests for admin-only authz across all `/admin/eval/*` routes, dataset-item CRUD, and comparison-run start/view (including the `partial`-status case); integration tests for the full comparison-run persistence flow and the admin-provisioning script; unit tests for the three evaluator functions (LLM judge mocked). All confirmed failing (404/ImportError) pre-implementation. Adds a `register_admin` conftest fixture.
2. **Backend** — `ComparisonRun` model + migration, `DatasetItem`/`ComparisonRunRequest`/`ComparisonRun` schemas, `admin_eval.py` routes (`require_admin`-gated) backed by `eval_service.py`. The `eval/` package implements the LangSmith side: `dataset_sync.py`, three LLM-as-judge evaluators, `targets.py` (wraps the live retrieval+generation pipeline as evaluate()'s target), and `run_experiment.py`. `backend/scripts/create_admin.py` provisions admin accounts out-of-band (no in-app signup path to that role).
3. **Frontend** — `adminEval.ts` API client, `AdminDashboard` component, `AdminEval` page (add benchmark questions, start/view comparison runs). `isAdmin` exposed on the auth context (decoded from the JWT, server still enforces `require_admin` on every route) gating the `/admin/eval` route and nav link.

Backend tests were run after each of the 3 commits (93 passing by the end, plus 8 `eval/tests` evaluator tests); frontend lint/build/test were run after subphase 3.

## Known gap (resolved)
Live LangSmith execution wasn't exercised in this environment initially (no LangSmith API key/credentials available, mirroring T062's live-Azure caveat from US2) — `run_experiment.py`'s use of `evaluate()` was only verified against the installed SDK's source rather than a live call.

A LangSmith API key is now available, and the manual step below was actually run against a real LangSmith dataset. Doing so surfaced two real bugs the mocked unit tests couldn't catch:
- `eval/evaluators/_llm_judge.py` sent `temperature=0` to the judge call, which the deployed chat model rejects (400: only the default of 1 is supported) — every evaluator call failed.
- `eval/targets.py`'s `target()` opens a fresh `asyncio.run()` loop per call, but `generation_service`/`retrieval_service` cache their async clients per process (correct for the app's single long-lived loop). Comparing a second version reused clients bound to the first version's now-closed loop, raising `RuntimeError: Event loop is closed`.

Both are fixed in a follow-up commit on this branch. Re-ran afterward with a real benchmark question against the live pipeline: two LangSmith experiments recorded, `had_failures: false`, real (non-zero) correctness/relevance/groundedness scores.

- [x] `cd backend && python -m pytest ../eval/tests` — 8 passed

- [x] `cd frontend && npm run lint && npm run test && npm run build`

## What

Adds a **provided-ID (identifier-input) benchmark mode** to the `studies/external_benchmarks` harness. **Harness-only** — no changes to biomapper2's core mapper/resolver. It exercises the *existing* `mapper.map_dataset_to_kg(provided_id_columns=..., annotation_mode='none')` feature in a new regime.

## Why

The existing name-input mode feeds the query string to BioMapper's name-resolution path. That is the wrong path for IDENTIFIER inputs: a bare Entrez/UniProt id fuzzy-matches to nonsense (`7525` → `USZIPCODE:75254`, 0%). Provided-ID mode instead gives BioMapper the **SOURCE** identifier as a provided id and measures whether its KG equivalence expansion reaches the **held-out TARGET** cross-ref — BioMapper's core cross-namespace-mapping capability, and the regime directly comparable to the incumbent ID-mapping tools.

## How

- **`config.ProvidedIdDatasetConfig`** — registry entry for provided-ID sets, with a fail-loud **anti-trivial-100% invariant** enforced in `__post_init__`: the scored TARGET can never be a provided column, and the source namespace must be disjoint from every target namespace (so a same-namespace round-trip cannot self-match).
- **`runner.run_provided_id`** — calls the mapper with `provided_id_columns=[source]`, `annotation_mode='none'` (pure provided-ID equivalence expansion, no name annotation), `vocab=None`. Anti-trivial `assert_target_held_out` runs **before** the mapper is called; the runtime guard is `mapped_to_kg_provided > 0` (the name-input `assigned>0` guard is inverted, since the assign path is off by design).
- **`scorers/provided_id_scorer.score_provided_id`** — correct iff the held-out gold TARGET CURIE is in BioMapper's returned equivalence set (`chosen_kg_id` + `kg_equivalent_ids`). Reuses `curie_scorer` helpers; reports Top-1 + coverage + precision/recall/F1 (same shape as the CURIE arm, so the campaign report renders it unchanged).
- **`adapters/provided_id`** — reshapes existing backbone/Hajjar bundles into source-provided + target-held-out form, reusing the streaming/reservoir-subsample + persisted-subsample reproducibility machinery.
- **`run.py`** — new `provided-id --dataset K --source S` CLI subcommand (legacy `--supplement` Hajjar flags preserved), so a gated run needs no hand-written driver.

### Datasets registered
| Dataset | Source (provided) | Target (held out) |
|---|---|---|
| `ncbi-gene2ensembl-provided-id` | Entrez GeneID (`NCBIGene`) | Ensembl |
| `uniprot-idmapping-provided-id` | UniProt accession (`UniProtKB`) | RefSeq / Ensembl |
| `hajjar-100-provided-id` | Hajjar curated ChEBI | InChIKey (structure) |

### How `annotation_mode` was set + anti-trivial verified
`map_dataset_to_kg` skips annotation entirely under `annotation_mode='none'` (verified against `annotation_engine.annotate` and `mapper.py`: mode `none` returns empty assigned IDs before the name field is ever read, and makes **no external annotation calls**). The provided source id flows normalize → link → resolve → `kg_equivalent_ids`, which is exactly the equivalence expansion we score. The anti-trivial invariant is enforced at **three** layers (config `__post_init__`, `runner` pre-mapper assertion, `scorer` pre-scoring assertion) and covered by tests that a target-in-provided / same-namespace-round-trip config **fails loud** rather than returning a silent 100%.

### Hajjar Table-2 parity cell
Metabolite anchor targets **ChEBI → InChIKey conversion accuracy** (`HAJJAR_PROVIDED_ID_PARITY_CELL`, `table_ref = "Hajjar et al. 2026, Table 2 — conversion accuracy to InChIKey from a provided compound identifier"`). Chosen over a ChEBI→ChEBI round-trip precisely because round-trip is trivial (source ns == target ns, rejected by the invariant). Per the Metabolon-96.5% scar, the published value is left `None` until transcribed from the paper at run time — no unverified number in source control.

## Tests
`studies/external_benchmarks` suite **98 → 120** (+22), all green. New coverage: provided-ID scorer known-input→expected, the fail-loud anti-trivial guard, adapters emitting source-provided + target-held-out, runner provided-path guard, and CLI/orchestrator wiring.

## Not done (by design)
The live benchmark was **not** run (code + PR only). Greptile-first (personal fork, base `dev`).

## Candidate biomapper2 finding (flagged, not fixed)
The metabolite anchor's correctness depends on the KG node carrying an `INCHIKEY:` entry in its `equivalent_ids` (Kestrel `/get-nodes`). If metabolite nodes expose InChIKey only via the structure-resolver path and **not** as a plain `equivalent_ids` cross-ref, ChEBI → InChIKey provided-ID reachability will read low despite correct linking — a provided-ID-expansion weakness to check against a live KG before interpreting the metabolite number.

items.title: fix(benchmarks): PLAN-0104 Step 1 — repair stale SQL_EXPECT and make its guard read the artifact
items.body:
## What

**PLAN-0104 Step 1.** Repairs two factually-wrong `SQL_EXPECT` gold tokens in the text-to-SQL comparison arm, and — the load-bearing half — makes the guard that was supposed to catch them actually able to fail. 2 files, +74/−3.

## The two tokens, and why nothing caught them

`SQL_EXPECT["nl-02"]` was `["11"]` and `["nl-05"]` was `["1"]`, against real values of **13** and **2**. PLAN-0070 added two synthetic readings (one warn-severity) and this constant was never updated. Because `score_sql` requires every expected token to appear in the stringified result, `"11"` can never appear in `"13"` — **both cases scored `wrong` on every run of this arm, silently.**

The reason it survived is the interesting part. `test_gold_values_cross_check_against_real_sql` has carried the docstring *"The SQL_EXPECT tokens are the true answers (validates the gold set)"* since session 58 — and its body **never referenced `SQL_EXPECT` at all**. It asserted `13`, `2`, `96.5`, `5`, `41.3` as literals beside the constant. Those assertions pin the *data*, which is genuinely useful, but nothing ever compared the constant *to* the data, so drift between them could not redden.

**A guard that reads its own copy of the answer cannot fail.**

## The fix keeps both layers rather than swapping one for the other

1. **Layer 1 (kept).** The literal assertions stay — they redden if `synthetic.py` moves.
2. **Layer 2 (new).** A hand-written correct SQL per question (`CANONICAL_SQL`) is executed, and the **real result rows are fed through the production `score_sql`**, asserting `correct`. A stale token now fails.

Layer 2 covers **every scored qid**, not the five the old test happened to touch, and asserts that coverage explicitly (`set(CANONICAL_SQL) == set(SQL_EXPECT) - HONESTY_QIDS`) so an uncovered qid cannot go stale the way nl-02 and nl-05 did. The honesty probe (nl-12) is scored from the error path, never from rows.

## Non-vacuity probe — run, and the RED seen, before any of this was trusted

Replanting `"nl-02": ["13"]` → `["11"]` (from a `/tmp` copy, **never restored from git**):

```
AssertionError: nl-02: SQL_EXPECT=['11'] does not match the real result [(13,)]
                — the gold token is stale, or the synthetic data moved
assert 'wrong' == 'correct'
tests/benchmark/test_nl_query_text_to_sql.py:147
```

The probe was designed so its result is informative, not merely red: **layer 1 stays green through this mutation** — execution reaches line 147 — which demonstrates that the OLD guard could not have caught this defect and that the new layer is what does. Restoration verified byte-identical; suite green again after.

## Deliberately NOT changed — `nl-03`, surfaced for Cray

Its token list omits `event-reading-08`, which `gold.yaml` lists among its three expected ids. **This is a different defect class.** `score_sql` matches a *subset*, so nl-03's present tokens are correct and it still scores `correct` — the oracle is **weaker than it should be, not wrong**. Adding the token would make the benchmark **stricter**: a model whose SQL filters by unit would flip nl-03 from `correct` to `wrong`. That changes what the measured numbers mean, which is a measurement decision rather than a typo fix, so it is not taken unilaterally.

Also noted and not acted on: `score_sql` matches tokens as **substrings**, so an expected `"1"` would match a result of `"21"`. Changing that alters the benchmark's semantics and is out of scope here.

## Verification — on the committed tree, `git diff --stat HEAD` empty

| Gate | Result |
|---|---|
| full `tests/` | **4028 passed, 8 skipped** (469s) |
| `mypy --strict services/` | Success, no issues in 134 source files |
| `ruff check .` | All checks passed |
| `ruff format --check .` | clean |

⚠️ ruff was run against `git archive HEAD` extracted to a temp dir — CI's actual view — because a bare `ruff check .` in the working directory also lints untracked local scratch files.

## Why this Step ran first

Step 7's live evidence run scores against this arm. Left stale, two of the twelve cases would have scored wrong on the very run the PLAN needs as its proof.

items.body:
Method-stream packet **E1** for Demo Report #1 (`docs/superpowers/plans/2026-08-11-demo-report-1-skill-ab-program.md`, Stage 2).

**Frame APPROVED by the operator.** Draft for one more round while the reviewer takes a delta pass. v0.4.

## Part 1 — Citation map

**21 URLs**, each fetched and confirmed to resolve and to say what is attributed to it. Primary sources for both mechanisms (agents.md / MIT; agentskills.io / Apache-2.0 + CC-BY-4.0; Claude Platform docs on the three progressive-disclosure levels), the live claim (Vercel's "AGENTS.md outperforms skills": 53/53/79/100, skill never invoked in 56% of default cases) and its 524-point HN thread, plus eight published empirical studies.

One search hit — the SWE-Skills-Bench artifact repo — returned **404** and is recorded as **not cited** rather than dropped silently. Six further search hits were not fetched and are listed as not cited.

**The gap:** every published controlled study varies *whether* instruction content is present, not *how* identical content is delivered. The two nearest studies vary organization *within* the skill mechanism. The most-read comparison changed content and mechanism together and did not state content equivalence.

## Part 2 — Approved comparison design

**Mechanism vs mechanism**: same agent, same model, same effort, same tasks, same instruction bytes; arm A = skill, arm B = AGENTS.md, arm C = neither.

| Decision | Outcome |
|---|---|
| Frame | Mechanism vs mechanism (public-skill on/off declined, kept as a second report) |
| Arms | **Three** — arm C is the manipulation check, with a pre-declared decision rule |
| Content | **`anthropics/skills`**, Apache-2.0, document skills excluded, per-subfolder license confirmed before lock |
| E4 pre-registration | **Committed**, conditional on the P5 e2e gate |

Byte identity: one frozen `source.md`, two packagings, three published digests, reader-reconstructable. MDE anchored at **~21 pp** with the derivation shown. Recomputability is a headline deliverable with a one-command recipe.

## Independent review applied (v0.3 → v0.4)

All four blocking findings were verified independently before fixing; all four were correct.

- **B1** — the literal top HN comment argues training-data scarcity; the confound objection comes from later commenters, and HN shows no per-comment scores. Three escalations corrected to "a dominant objection in the thread."
- **B2** — "attested-not-graded per the program's global constraints" was mis-attributed (the program says effort is an *enforced* pinning key). Replaced with the verified truth: the pin gates dispatch, but `verifyRunPinning` checks harness/model/loadout only and `PinningAxis` excludes effort, so applied reasoning depth is attested only.
- **B3** — the work-directory placement leg is **not** on existing precedent at head; the loadout routes to the input root at every site. Downgraded to "must be confirmed by P2's acceptance gate." The `--plugin-dir` half **is** confirmed and labeled as such.
- **B4** — the 20–26 pp band was not derivable from the cited numbers. Derivation now shown: anchor ~21 pp, decline the 47 pp gap (56% of those runs never invoked the skill), 18–36 pp as corroboration.

**New finding surfaced by review (M2), handed to P2 and E3:** arm B's `AGENTS.md` sits **inside the task's git working tree** on a SWE slate — visible to `git status`/`git diff` and able to contaminate patch extraction. Exclusion required and verified, not assumed.

## Open items

1. **Publication framing** — operator's call, narrowed to prominence and tone (the MDE anchoring cites Vercel regardless). Deferrable to E5.
2. **Pinning symmetry** — re-scoped, resolved by **P2's acceptance gate**, not the operator. Escalates only if P2 reports the mechanism needs a platform change.

Also gate-resolved, not operator-resolved: arm C's pinning mechanic, decided from E2 preview evidence of behavioral identity to a true no-file run (an empty loadout still materializes a file, so the baseline validity question is real). The `unverifiable` allowance is named as a **disclosed departure** from P2's every-axis-enforced gate.

## Constraints honored

No product-implemented statistics — no estimator proposed; numbers come from the method registry. Effort held constant, with its verification status stated exactly. `jinn.skill.v1` cited for grounding only; no engineering designed.

items.title: Record that goja has no heap limit, and correct two stale scores
items.body:
Two gaps in the "Why not goja?" section, both found while merging #4.

## goja has no heap limit

The comparison table has always claimed an out-of-memory is catchable under
goant and fatal under goja, but nothing in the README said *why*. Checked
against the goja version the benchmarks use: its `Runtime` exposes
`SetMaxCallStackSize`, which bounds recursion depth, and nothing that bounds
memory.

So a script that retains more than the host can give it allocates until the Go
runtime cannot satisfy an allocation — and Go's out-of-memory is a runtime throw
rather than a panic: no `recover`, no deferred anything, and every other
goroutine in the process goes with it. That is the same failure that took V8
down for us, reached by a different road.

For a robot runtime sharing one process between customers' scripts this matters
as much as the language gap, so it now sits where someone weighing the two
engines will actually read it, linked to
[What the memory limit counts](#what-the-memory-limit-counts) from #4.

## Two stale scores

"Why not goja?" and "Where it came from" both still read **42,620 of 42,758
against goja's 33,304**. Those predate the iterator-helper work and the
skip-list change; the Conformance table was updated and these two were missed.

All three now agree: **42,739 of 42,740 against goja's 33,303**, same checkout,
same harness.

Documentation only — no code changes.
